titleStmt.title: The EDF scheduling of sporadic task systems on uniform multiprocessors *

analytic.title: The EDF scheduling of sporadic task systems on uniform multiprocessors *

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The global EDF scheduling of sporadic task systems upon uniform multiprocessor platforms is studied. A sufficient schedulability test is presented and proved correct. It is shown that this test generalizes the previously-known exact uniprocessor, and sufficient identical multiprocessor, EDFschedulability tests.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: A multiprocessor computer platform is comprised of several processors. A platform in which all the processors have the same capabilities is referred to as an identical multiprocessor, while those in which different processors have different capabilities are called heterogeneous multiprocessors. Heterogeneous multiprocessors may be further classified into uniform and unrelated multiprocessors. The only difference between the different processors in a uniform multiprocessor is the rate at which they can execute work: each processor is characterized by a speed or computing capacity s parameter and any job executing on the processor for t time units completes t × s units of execution. In unrelated multiprocessors, on the other hand, the amount of execution completed by a particular job executing on a given processor depends upon the identities of both the job and the processor.

A real-time system is often modeled as a finite collection of independent recurrent tasks, each of which generates a potentially infinite sequence of jobs. Every job is characterized by an arrival time, an execution requirement, and a deadline, and it is required that a job completes execution between its arrival time and its deadline. Different formal models for recurring tasks place different restrictions on the values of the parameters of jobs generated by each task. One of the more commonly used formal models is the sporadic task model [30,13]. Each recurrent task τ i in this model is characterized by three parameters: τ i = (C i , D i , T i ), with the interpretation that τ i may generate an infinite sequence of jobs with successive jobs arriving at least T i time units apart, each with an execution requirement at most C i and a deadline D i time-units after its arrival time. A sporadic task system τ is comprised of a finite collection of such sporadic tasks. Sporadic task systems in which each task is required to have its relative deadline and period parameters the same (D i = T i for all i) are called implicit-deadline task systems, and ones in which each task is required to have its relative deadline be no larger than its period parameter (D i ≤ T i for all i) are called constraineddeadline task systems.

Several results have been obtained over the past decade, concerning the scheduling of implicit-deadline systems on identical [10,31,29,2,1,26,28] and on uniform [25,8,24,11,23,18,3,4] multiprocessors, and of constraineddeadline systems on identical multiprocessors [5,6,14,15,16,20,9] (see also Section 4 for a further discussion on related work). This paper seeks to extend this body of work, by addressing the scheduling of constrained-deadline sporadic task systems upon uniform multiprocessors. We assume that the platform is fully preemptive, -an executing job may be interrupted at any instant in time and have its execution resumed later with no cost or penalty. We study the behavior of the well-known Earliest Deadline First scheduling algorithm [27,19] when scheduling systems of sporadic tasks upon such preemptive platforms. We assume that the platform allows for global inter-processor migration -a job may begin execution on any processor and a preempted job may resume execution on the same processor as, or a different processor from, the one it had been executing on prior to preemption. (However, each job may execute on at most one processor at each instant in time.) We will refer to Earliest Deadline First scheduling with global inter-processor migration as global EDF (or simply EDF).

Contributions. We obtain a new test -to our knowledge, this is the first such test -for determining whether a given constrained-deadline sporadic task system is guaranteed to be scheduled to meet all deadlines upon a specified uniform multiprocessor platform, when scheduled using EDF. This test is derived by integrating and generalizing techniques that have previously been used for schedulability analysis of constrained-deadline task systems on identical multiprocessors, and for the schedulability analysis of implicit-deadline task systems on uniform multiprocessors. This synthesis turned out to be quite non-trivial, in that several new proof and derivation techniques were needed. We hope that these new techniques will be useful in further extending multiprocessor real-time schedule theory to be applicable to uniform (and ultimately, unrelated) multiprocessors.

Organization. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we formally define the sporadic task model and uniform multiprocessors platforms, and provide some additional useful definitions, notation, and terminology concerning sporadic tasks and uniform multiprocessors. We also briefly discuss how global EDF is to be implemented upon uniform multiprocessors. In Section 3 we derive, and prove the correctness of, a schedulability test for determining whether a given constrained-deadline sporadic task system is EDF-schedulable on a specified uniform multiprocessor platform. In Section 4, we briefly discuss the research that our work build on -scheduling implicit-deadline task systems on uniform multiprocessors, and scheduling constrained-deadline task systems on identical multiprocessors.

2. Task and platform model §1. Sporadic task systems. A sporadic task τ i = (C i , D i , T i ) is characterized by a worst-case execution requirement C i , a (relative) deadline D i , and a minimum inter-arrival separation parameter T i , also referred to as the period of the task. Such a sporadic task generates a potentially infinite sequence of jobs, with successive job-arrivals separated by at least T i time units. Each job has a worstcase execution requirement equal to C i and a deadline that occurs D i time units after its arrival time. We refer to the interval, of size D i , between such a job's arrival instant and deadline as its scheduling window. We assume a fully preemptive execution model: any executing job may be interrupted at any instant in time, and its execution resumed later with no cost or penalty. A sporadic task system is comprised of a finite number of such sporadic tasks. Let τ denote a system of such sporadic tasks: τ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . τ n }, with τ i = (C i , D i , T i ) for all i, 1 ≤ i ≤ n. Task system τ is said to be a constrained sporadic task system if it is guaranteed that each task τ i ∈ τ has its relative deadline parameter no larger than its period: D i ≤ T i for all τ i ∈ τ . We restrict our attention here to constrained task systems.
We find it convenient to define some properties and parameters for individual sporadic tasks, and for sporadic task systems.

div.head: Utilization:
div.p: The utilization u i of a task τ i is the ratio C i /T i of its execution requirement to its period. The total utilization u sum (τ ) and the largest utilization u max (τ ) of a task system τ are defined as follows:
div.formula: u sum (τ ) def = τi∈τ u i ; u max (τ ) def = max τi∈τ (u i ) Density:
div.p: The density δ i of a task τ i is the ratio C i /D i of its execution requirement to its relative deadline. The total density δ sum (τ ) and the largest density δ max (τ ) of a task system τ are defined as follows:
div.formula: δ sum (τ ) def = τi∈τ δ i ; δ max (τ ) def = max τi∈τ (δ i )
div.p: DBF: For any interval length t, the demand bound function DBF(τ i , t) of a sporadic task τ i bounds the maximum cumulative execution requirement by jobs of τ i that both arrive in, and have deadlines within, any interval of length t. It has been shown [13] that
div.formula: DBF(τ i , t) = max 0, ( t -D i T i + 1) C i
div.p: Load: A load parameter, based upon the DBF function, may be defined for any sporadic task system τ as follows:
div.formula: LOAD(τ ) def = max t>0 τi∈τ DBF(τ i , t) t
div.p: Computing DBF (and thereby, LOAD) will turn out to be a critical component of the schedulability analysis test proposed in this paper; hence, it is important that DBF be efficiently computable if this schedulability test is to be efficiently implementable as claimed. Fortunately, computing DBF is a well-studied subject, and algorithms are known for computing DBF exactly [13,32], or approximately to any arbitrary degree of accuracy [7,22,21] in pseudo-polynomial or polynomial time respectively. §2. Uniform multiprocessors. A uniform multiprocessor π = (s 1 , s 2 , . . . , s m ) is comprised of m ≥ 1 processors, with the i'th processor characterized by speed or computing capacity s i . The interpretation is that a job executing on the i'th processor for a duration of t units of time completes t × s i units of execution. Without loss of generality, we assume that the speeds are specified in non-decreasing order: s i ≥ s i+1 for all i. We will also use the following notation:
div.formula: S i (π) def = i j=1 s j .(1)
div.p: That is, S i (π) denotes the cumulative computing capacity of the i fastest processors in π (consequently, S m (π) denotes the total computing capacity of π).
An additional parameter that turns out to be useful in describing the properties of a uniform multiprocessor is the "lambda" parameter [24,25]:
div.formula: λ(π) def = m max i=1 m j=i+1 s j s i .(2)
div.p: This parameter ranges in value between 0 and (m-1) for an m-processor uniform multiprocessor platform, with a value of (m -1) corresponding to the degenerate case when all the processors are of the same speed (i.e., the platform is an identical multiprocessor). §3. Earliest Deadline First scheduling. Priority-driven scheduling algorithms operate on uniform multiprocessors as follows: at each instant in time they assign a priority to each job that is awaiting execution, and favor for execution the jobs with the greatest priorities. Specifically, (i) no processor is idled while there is an active job awaiting execution; (ii) when there are fewer active jobs than processors, the jobs execute on the fastest processors and the slowest ones are idled; and (iii) greater-priority jobs execute on the faster processors. The Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling algorithm [27,19] is a priority-driven scheduling algorithm that assigns priority to jobs according to their (absolute) deadlines: the earlier the deadline, the greater the priority.

With respect to a given platform, a given sporadic task system is said to be feasible if there exists a schedule meeting all deadlines for every collection of jobs that may be generated by the task system. A given sporadic task system is said to be (global) EDF schedulable if EDF meets all deadlines for every collection of jobs that may be generated by the task system.

div.head: A global-EDF schedulability test

Our approach towards developing this test follows the same general framework as the derivations of sufficient schedulability tests on identical multiprocessor systems: we obtain necessary conditions for global EDF to miss a deadline when scheduling sporadic task system τ upon uniform multiprocessor platform π. By taking the contrapositive of these conditions, we obtain a sufficient schedulability condition.

Observe that µ and ν are functions of both λ(π) and δ max (τ ); thus, Theorem 1 uses the parameter λ(π) of the uniform multiprocessor platform π, and the parameters LOAD(τ ) and δ max (τ ) of sporadic task system τ in order to determine whether the system is EDF-schedulable. In other words, the parameters of the individual tasks comprising the task system are distilled into the two composite parameters LOAD and δ max , while the platform characteristics are distilled into the parameter λ. The guarantee is that all systems τ whose (LOAD(τ ), δ max (τ )) parameters satisfy the condition of the theorem for a platform π with given λ(π) value are guaranteed EDF-schedulable while systems whose parameters do not satisfy this condition may or may not be EDF-schedulable.

Evaluation. As stated in Section 2, λ(π) takes on a value between 0 and m -1 where m denotes the number of processors in π, with λ(π) = m -1 denoting an identical multiprocessor. Informally, the "smallness" of parameter λ(π) -the closer it is to zero -can be taken to denote the degree by which π is different from being an identical multiprocessor: it would be smallest in a platform in which each processor has a very different speed (all the s j 's are very distinct). For a given S m (π) -i.e., a given total computing capacity -it follows from Equation 5 that µ is larger for smaller λ(π). Similarly, it follows from the definition of ν (Equation 10) that platforms in which the fastest processors have significantly more computing capacity than the others will have smaller µ; intuitively, this means (Lemma 2) that such platforms will have fewer carry-in jobs whose work contributions need to be accounted for. We therefore conclude, based on Equation 11 in Theorem 1 above, that the further removed a uniform multiprocessor platform is from "identicalness" (as quantified by its λ parameter), the superior its ability to schedule sporadic task systems according to the EDF-schedulability test of Theorem 1. This result is in keeping with similar results obtained for the scheduling of of implicit-deadline task systems (see Section 4 below), where, too, it was observed that for a given cumulative computing capacity better performance is obtained for platforms in which the processors have very different speeds.

Generalization of the identical multiprocessor test from [9]. It turns out that by setting λ(π) = (m -1), Theorem 1 reduces to the EDF-schedulability test for identical multiprocessors derived in [9]. It consequently follows that our test here is a generalization of the identical multiprocessor EDF-schedulability test from [9].
Exact test for uniprocessors. The test of Theorem 1 is easily seen to be exact (necessary and sufficient) for uniprocessors;
Corollary 1 The test of Theorem 1 is exact for uniprocessors.

Proof: For m = 1, it is easily seen (Equation 2) that λ(π) evaluates to zero. From Equation 5and Equation 10, it follows that µ equals the total computing capacity of the uniprocessor (S m (π) is, by definition, the total computing capacity of the uniprocessor platform) and ν = 0 (there are no carry-ins). Consequently, the RHS of the condition in Theorem 1 evaluates to the total computing capacity of the platform, and the schedulability condition becomes that LOAD(τ ) should not exceed the computing capacity of the processor -this is exactly the uniprocessor preemptive EDF-schedulability test from, e.g., [13].

div.head: Related Work
div.p: There are very few works about the scheduling of recurrent constrained-deadline task systems on uniform multiprocessors. In [17] the authors consider the global scheduling of periodic tasks on uniform multiprocessors and provide an exact schedulability test for static-priority global schedulers. However, these results are only valid for periodic task systems and do not generalize to sporadic task systems. To the best of our knowledge, other works concern either the scheduling of sporadic implicit-deadline systems on uniform multiprocessors or sporadic constrained-deadline systems on identical multiprocessor. We will briefly review some of this literature below.

div.head: Implicit-deadline on uniform multiprocessors
div.p: Reference [8] addresses the scheduling of sporadic tasks on uniform multiprocessors. It is shown that in the absence of the Integer Boundary Constraint (IBC) [8], the feasibility-analysis of n implicit-deadline tasks on an mprocessor uniform multiprocessor platform can be done in O(n + m log n) time; in the presence of the IBC the same feasibility problem is NP-hard. This paper also studies a tractable special case, light systems, where the utilization of the heaviest task u max is no more than the execution capacity s m of the slowest processor. For light systems [8] provides a necessary and sufficient feasibility test.

References [24,25] provide an exact (i.e., necessary and sufficient) test for determining whether a given implicitdeadline sporadic task system is feasible on a uniform platform π that is specified only by its λ(π) parameter (Definition 2) and its cumulative computing capacity S m (π). The authors apply this exact feasibility test to derive a sufficient condition for a sporadic task system to successfully meet all deadlines when scheduled using global EDF.

Reference [12] considers the scheduling of implicitdeadline sporadic task systems using global Rate-Monotonic and provides a simple, sufficient test and a static-priority scheduling algorithm that adopts the global approach for determining whether any given sporadic task system will be successfully scheduled by algorithm RM upon a given uniform multiprocessor platform. The simple test is based again on the λ(π) parameter and the total capacity S m (π) of a uniform multiprocessor platform π.

Reference [23] considers the EDF partitioning of sporadic tasks. The paper provides a partitioning algorithm and a utilization-based condition for determining whether a given system of sporadic tasks is successfully scheduled upon any specified uniform multiprocessor platform.

Reference [18] considers the partitioning of sporadic tasks. The authors derive the minimum limit on the utilization bounds when greedy algorithm is used to partition the task set and RM is used on each individual processor. They also derive a utilization bound for the partition algorithm that performs allocations according to decreasing order of task utilizations.
Reference [3] considers the EDF partitioning of sporadic tasks and proves that its speed competitive ratio is at most three (while the speed competitive ratio of [23,18] is infinite).
Reference [4] considers the RM partitioning of sporadic tasks and proves that its speed competitive ratio is at most 1 + √ 2.

div.head: Constrained-deadline on identical multiprocessors
div.p: In [5] Baker presents schedulability tests for global EDF and global RM scheduling of sporadic tasks. The paper presents also a new framework to design multiprocessor schedulability tests, to summarize, the idea is to consider a task which misses its deadline and bound the interference of the other jobs, i.e., the cumulative instants where all processors are busy for these higher priority jobs.
In [6] Baker completes the previous study and focuses on EDF, extends the results and shows that an algorithm denoted EDF-US[1/2] is optimal.

In [14] Bertogna, Cirinei, and Lipari propose an improved (as compared to [5,6]) schedulability test for global EDF that is able to successfully guarantee a larger portion of schedulable task sets, paricularly in the case of "heavy" tasks. In [15] they apply similar techniques to global DM scheduling. This work extends and improves [5] particularly in the presence of heavy tasks.
Based on [5,14] Cirinei and Baker consider the global EDZL scheduler in [16]. The authors design a sufficient schedulability test and show that EDZL is superior to pure EDF.

Reference [9] derives a new test for determining whether a given sporadic task system is guaranteed to be scheduled to meet all deadlines upon a specified computing platform, when scheduled using global EDF. The test characterizes a task set by its LOAD and δ max parameters. The authors prove that its speed competitive ratio is 2/(3 -√ 5).

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: Most research on multiprocessor real-time scheduling has focused on the simplest model -systems of implicitdeadline tasks that are scheduled on identical multiprocessors. More recent research has attempted to generalize this work in two different directions, by either generalizing the task model (to constrained-deadline and arbitrarydeadline sporadic task systems), or by generalizing the processor model (to uniform and unrelated multiprocessors). To our knowledge, this is the first piece of work that generalizes along both the task-model and the processor axes, by considering the scheduling of constrained-deadline sporadic task systems upon uniform multiprocessors.

We have obtained a new schedulability test for the global EDF scheduling of constrained sporadic task systems upon preemptive uniform multiprocessor platforms. This test characterizes a task system by its LOAD and δ max parameters, and a platform by its total computing capacity and its λ parameter.

div.p: We believe that we have gained valuable insights into the global scheduling process upon uniform multiprocessors; based on these insights, we have introduced novel analysis techniques. We are optimistic that these analysis techniques introduced here will prove useful in studying uniform multiprocessor global schedulability for many different scheduling algorithms and for more general task models.
